title: Gram Stain Steps and the Novobiocin Fork for S. saprophyticus
summary: Learn the four Gram stain steps and why the decolorizer decides the result, what makes gram-positive cells look pink, and how novobiocin resistance points to Staphylococcus saprophyticus among coagulase-negative staphylococci in urine.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 57 Hit 35 (Gram stain order and the decolorizer), Hit 9 (S. saprophyticus, novobiocin-resistant CoNS of UTI) and Exam Trap 1 (novobiocin trap), checked against Li 2020, Vijayakumar 2023 and Mitra 2023 (Gram stain), and Becker 2014, Vickers 2007, De Paulis 2003 (read via a page-fetch tool) and Lawal 2021 (S. saprophyticus). Exam Trap 1 calls S. saprophyticus the "lone reversal" among common CoNS; De Paulis 2003 and Becker 2014 list the S. cohnii group (and S. xylosus) as novobiocin-resistant too, so the lesson teaches novobiocin resistance as presumptive (register flag rv-novobiocin-not-unique). Not taught: zone-diameter breakpoints, acid-fast staining, MALDI-TOF identification of CoNS, treatment.

objectives: List the four Gram stain reagents in order and explain why the decolorizer step is critical.
Name causes that make gram-positive organisms look gram-negative and the corrective action.
Use novobiocin susceptibility to presumptively identify Staphylococcus saprophyticus, and state its limits.

scenes.title: Pink cocci and no zone
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a urine culture from a 21-year-old woman with dysuria grows catalase-positive, coagulase-negative cocci. (1) A Gram stain made from the colonies after the plate sat on the bench for 3 days shows a mix of purple and pink cocci. (2) A fresh repeat smear was stained with a long acetone rinse and the cocci look pink. (3) A 5-µg novobiocin disk shows growth right up to the disk. Question token: “Gram-negative cocci, or a staining error? And which staphylococcus?”

cues.text: A young woman with painful urination. Her urine grows catalase-positive, coagulase-negative cocci.
A smear from a three-day-old plate shows purple and pink cocci, and a smear given a long decolorizer rinse looks pink. The novobiocin disk shows no zone at all.
Are these gram-negative cocci, or a staining error? And which staphylococcus is it?

scenes.title: Four steps, one critical
scenes.altText: Schematic: four reagent cards in order. (1) Crystal violet, a positively charged basic dye, stains all cells purple. (2) Gram’s iodine, the mordant, forms a crystal violet–iodine complex. (3) Decolorizer (acetone, ethanol or an acetone–alcohol mixture; acetone is the fastest) dissolves the complex out of gram-negative cells, whose thin peptidoglycan is perforated, while the thick peptidoglycan of gram-positive cells holds it. (4) Safranin counterstain turns the decolorized gram-negative cells pink-red; gram-positive cells stay purple.

cues.text: Step one: crystal violet, a positively charged dye, stains every cell purple. Step two: Gram’s iodine, the mordant, locks the dye into a crystal violet and iodine complex.
Step three is the decolorizer: acetone, alcohol, or a mix. Acetone works fastest. It washes the complex out of gram-negative cells, whose thin peptidoglycan layer is breached.
Gram-positive cells keep the purple complex, trapped in their thick peptidoglycan wall.
Step four: the safranin counterstain colors the now colorless gram-negative cells pink-red. Purple means gram-positive. Pink means gram-negative.

scenes.title: When gram-positives look pink
scenes.altText: Error card: decolorization is the most important step; over-decolorization can make gram-positive organisms look gram-negative, and under-decolorization the reverse. Factors card: old cultures (cells older than about 24 h) lose gram-positivity and can look gram-negative or gram-variable; excessive heat during fixation damages the cell wall; thick or crowded smears decolorize unevenly; too much counterstain can displace the complex. Fix card: if decolorization is in doubt, decolorize the whole smear and restain, and repeat from a fresh culture.

cues.text: Decolorization is the step that makes or breaks a Gram stain. Too much, and gram-positive organisms lose the purple and are misread as gram-negative. Too little, and gram-negative organisms stay purple.
The cell wall matters too. Cultures older than about a day lose their gram-positivity and can look gram-negative or gram-variable. Too much heat during fixing damages the wall in the same way.
Thick or crowded smears decolorize unevenly, and leaving the counterstain on too long can push out the purple complex.
If the colors make no sense, decolorize the whole slide and restain it, and repeat the stain from a fresh culture.

scenes.title: The novobiocin fork in coagulase-negative staphylococci
scenes.altText: CoNS card: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is the second most frequent cause of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection in young, sexually active women (Becker 2014); one source cites it as the cause of uncomplicated UTI in 10–20% of young women (Lawal 2021). Novobiocin card (5-µg disk): S. saprophyticus is intrinsically resistant (a novobiocin-resistant form of its GyrB target); the S. epidermidis group is susceptible. Not unique: S. cohnii subsp. cohnii, the S. cohnii group (S. xylosus, S. cohnii subsp. urealyticum) and S. hominis subsp. novobiosepticus are also novobiocin-resistant; one five-test scheme separates them with mannose (S. saprophyticus group negative, S. cohnii group positive) and trehalose (positive confirms S. saprophyticus) (De Paulis 2003). Hook answers: (1–2) pink cocci from an old plate or after a long rinse = suspect staining error; restain a fresh culture; (3) novobiocin-resistant CoNS in urine from a young woman = presumptive S. saprophyticus.

cues.text: Among coagulase-negative staphylococci, Staphylococcus saprophyticus is the classic urinary one. It is a leading cause of uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection in young, sexually active women.
A five microgram novobiocin disk splits the group. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is naturally resistant, because its drug target, GyrB, is a resistant form. The epidermidis group is susceptible.
But resistance is not unique to it: the cohnii group, including xylosus, is resistant too. So identification schemes add tests such as mannose and trehalose.

Back to the hook. Pink cocci from an old plate or a long rinse suggest a staining error, so restain a fresh culture. A novobiocin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococcus in this patient’s urine is presumptively saprophyticus.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Pink cocci on an old plate are gram-negative cocci” (✓ old cultures and over-decolorization make gram-positives look pink — restain a fresh culture); “S. saprophyticus is novobiocin-susceptible” (✓ it is resistant; S. epidermidis is susceptible); “Novobiocin resistance alone identifies S. saprophyticus” (✓ the S. cohnii group is resistant too; add other tests).

cues.text: Trap one: pink cocci from an old plate are gram-negative. No: old cells and too much decolorizer make gram-positives look pink.
Trap two: saprophyticus is novobiocin-susceptible. No: it is resistant. Epidermidis is the susceptible one.
Trap three: novobiocin resistance alone proves saprophyticus. No: the cohnii group is resistant too.

props.title: ✗ “Novobiocin R alone = S. saprophyticus.”
lines: ✓ S. cohnii group is resistant too

scenes.title: Come In, Don’t Stay
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Come In, Don’t Stay” — Crystal violet, Iodine, Decolorizer, Safranin; and the decolorizer must not stay too long. Second line: “Sapro Shrugs off novobiocin.” Tokens: C-I-D-S order · decolorizer briefly · Sapro resistant. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: Come In, Don’t Stay. Crystal violet, Iodine, Decolorizer, Safranin, and don’t let the decolorizer stay too long. And saprophyticus shrugs off novobiocin.

Where it breaks: the phrase gives the order, not the timing, which depends on the decolorizer and smear thickness. Some organisms stain gram-variable even when done well. And other coagulase-negative species also shrug off novobiocin.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Crystal violet → iodine → decolorizer (critical) → safranin · old cultures or over-decolorizing make gram-positives look pink”, “Staphylococcus saprophyticus: novobiocin-resistant CoNS of UTI in young women · S. epidermidis susceptible · S. cohnii group also resistant”.

cues.text: In the Gram stain the decolorizer is the critical step, so pink cocci from an old culture or a long rinse need a fresh restain, and a novobiocin-resistant coagulase-negative staphylococcus in a young woman’s urine is presumptively Staphylococcus saprophyticus.

props.label: Novobiocin R CoNS in UTI → presumptive S. saprophyticus

explanation.what: Plain language: the Gram stain dyes every bacterium purple, then washes the dye out of the thin-walled ones and colors them pink. If the wash goes too far, or the cells are old and damaged, purple bacteria turn pink by mistake. Among coagulase-negative staphylococci, a simple antibiotic disk, novobiocin, flags the species that causes bladder infections in young women. Scientific terms: crystal violet (primary stain), Gram’s iodine (mordant), crystal violet–iodine complex, decolorizer (acetone, ethanol, acetone–alcohol), safranin (counterstain), peptidoglycan, over- and under-decolorization, gram-variable, coagulase-negative staphylococci (CoNS), intrinsic novobiocin resistance (GyrB).
explanation.why: Gram-positive cells hold the dye–iodine complex in a thick peptidoglycan wall; gram-negative cells, with a thin wall, lose it to the decolorizer. Anything that thins or damages the wall, or prolongs decolorization, removes the complex from gram-positive cells. S. saprophyticus carries a naturally novobiocin-resistant form of the GyrB target, while S. epidermidis and most common CoNS are susceptible.
explanation.measure: Order: crystal violet → Gram’s iodine → decolorizer → safranin. Decolorize briefly and watch it; acetone is fastest. Old cultures (older than about 24 h), heat damage, thick smears and excess counterstain cause errors; when in doubt, decolorize the whole smear and restain, from a fresh culture. Novobiocin 5-µg disk: S. saprophyticus resistant, S. epidermidis group susceptible; the S. cohnii group (and S. hominis subsp. novobiosepticus) is also resistant, so add tests such as mannose and trehalose (or another identification method).
explanation.differs: Over-decolorization (gram-positives look pink) vs under-decolorization (gram-negatives look purple); S. saprophyticus (novobiocin-resistant, urinary) vs S. epidermidis (novobiocin-susceptible); S. saprophyticus vs S. cohnii group (both novobiocin-resistant; separated by other tests).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: order the Gram stain reagents, name the critical step, explain pink gram-positive cocci from an old culture, or pick S. saprophyticus for a novobiocin-resistant CoNS in urine from a young woman.

comparisons.title: Over- vs under-decolorization
comparisons.distinguisher: Which way the decolorizer error pushed the color; restain to settle it.

comparisons.title: S. saprophyticus vs S. epidermidis
comparisons.distinguisher: Novobiocin disk result, supported by other identification tests.

mnemonic.text: “Come In, Don’t Stay”: Crystal violet, Iodine, Decolorizer, Safranin — and don’t let the decolorizer stay too long. “Sapro shrugs off novobiocin.”
mnemonic.explanation: Gives the reagent order, the critical step, and the novobiocin direction.
mnemonic.limitation: The phrase gives order, not timing (which varies with decolorizer and smear thickness); some organisms stain gram-variable even when the stain is done well; other CoNS (the S. cohnii group) are also novobiocin-resistant.

analogyLimitations: Smears and disks are drawn as schematic cards, not real images.
Novobiocin resistance is a presumptive marker, not a full identification.

questions.stem: Which sequence of Gram stain reagents is correct?

options.text: Crystal violet, Gram’s iodine, decolorizer, safranin
options.rationale: Correct. Primary stain, mordant, decolorizer, then counterstain.

options.text: Safranin, decolorizer, crystal violet, Gram’s iodine
options.rationale: Incorrect. Safranin is the counterstain and comes last.

options.text: Crystal violet, decolorizer, Gram’s iodine, safranin
options.rationale: Incorrect. Iodine must form the dye–iodine complex before decolorizing.

options.text: Gram’s iodine, crystal violet, safranin, decolorizer
options.rationale: Incorrect. Decolorizing after the counterstain would remove it, and the mordant follows the primary stain.

questions.stem: Catalase-positive cocci in clusters from a 3-day-old plate stain a mix of pink and purple. What is the best next step?

options.text: Repeat the Gram stain on a fresh (overnight) culture
options.rationale: Correct. Old cultures lose gram-positivity and can look gram-negative or gram-variable.
Incorrect. Pink cells from an old culture may be gram-positives that lost the complex.

options.text: Lengthen the decolorizer step on the repeat
options.rationale: Incorrect. More decolorizer would make gram-positive cells look even more pink.

options.text: Skip the iodine step to reduce background
options.rationale: Incorrect. Without the mordant, the dye is easily washed out of gram-positive cells.

questions.stem: A coagulase-negative staphylococcus from the urine of a 20-year-old woman with cystitis grows up to the edge of a 5-µg novobiocin disk. Which statement is best?

options.text: It is presumptively S. saprophyticus; confirm with further tests
options.rationale: Correct. S. saprophyticus is intrinsically novobiocin-resistant and causes UTI in young women; other resistant CoNS exist, so confirm.
Incorrect. The S. epidermidis group is novobiocin-susceptible.

options.text: Novobiocin resistance proves S. saprophyticus with no other test
options.rationale: Incorrect. The S. cohnii group is also novobiocin-resistant.

options.text: It must be S. aureus because it is resistant
options.rationale: Incorrect. The isolate is coagulase-negative, and S. aureus is naturally novobiocin-susceptible.

Reagent order (crystal violet, iodide, acetone–ethanol decolorant, safranin O); mechanism (dye–mordant complex retained by thick peptidoglycan, dissolved from perforated thin peptidoglycan of gram-negatives); more decolorant gave more over-decolorized smears; gram-positives in decline phase stain heterogeneously.

references.citation: Vijayakumar T, Divya B, Vasanthi V, Narayan M, Kumar AR, Krishnan R. Diagnostic Utility of Gram Stain for Oral Smears - A Review. J Microsc Ultrastruct. 2023;11(3):130-134. doi:10.4103/jmau.jmau_108_22

Reagent roles; acetone fastest decolorizer, then ethanol; old cultures (> 24 h) and excessive heat make gram-positives look gram-negative; crowded smears decolorize improperly; excessive counterstaining; decolorization must be monitored to avoid under- or over-decolorization; gram-variable organisms.

claims.text: Gram stain reagent order and roles; mechanism of retention by thick peptidoglycan.
Decolorization is the critical step; over-decolorization makes gram-positives look gram-negative and under-decolorization the reverse; restain when in doubt.
Old cultures, heat damage, crowded smears and excess counterstain cause Gram stain errors.
S. saprophyticus is a leading cause of uncomplicated UTI in young, sexually active women (10–20% in one source).

S. saprophyticus is intrinsically novobiocin-resistant (GyrB); S. epidermidis group susceptible; S. cohnii group and S. hominis subsp. novobiosepticus also resistant; mannose and trehalose help confirm.
Scenario invented; smears and disks schematic.
“Come In, Don’t Stay”; “Sapro shrugs off novobiocin.”

accuracyFlags.issue: Exam Trap 1 says S. saprophyticus is the "lone reversal" among common CoNS for novobiocin. De Paulis 2003 and Becker 2014 (Table 2) list the S. cohnii group and S. xylosus as novobiocin-resistant too, (and De Paulis 2003 also lists S. hominis subsp. novobiosepticus), so novobiocin resistance is presumptive and needs confirmation (for example mannose and trehalose in the De Paulis scheme; urease does not separate the S. saprophyticus and S. cohnii groups there). The lesson teaches it that way. See register flag rv-novobiocin-not-unique.

Becker 2014, Vickers 2007 and De Paulis 2003 were read through a page-fetch tool that returns summarised and quoted passages, not as downloaded full text; for Becker 2014 only the first part of the article and Table 2 were read.

morphology.note: No micrographs; smears and disks shown as cards.
